You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.

# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: transform the black DVD into a white DVD
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image visibly show the source item near the center changed from black to white, with enough visual correspondence to identify it as the same item?
node.criteria: Pass only if the source item can be matched to an edited object and that object is visibly white rather than black. Fail if the source item is confidently matched and remains black, or is absent without evidence of the requested recoloring. Unknown if correspondence or the relevant color cannot be determined from the images. Do not count a newly appearing white disc as progress without evidence it is the source item.
node.binding: Compare the small printed rectangular item near the center of the source with edited objects using position, shape, and surrounding scene context. Consider both white discs as candidates, but do not assume either is the source item; scene changes may limit correspondence. Judge visible color change only for a confidently matched item, and use unknown when correspondence remains unresolved.

node_traces.evidence: The source has a small printed rectangular item near the center. In the edited image, that item is no longer visibly identifiable; two white discs appear, one near the center and one beside the dark object on the right. The scene and object layout have changed, so neither disc can be confidently matched to the source item. Their whiteness alone does not establish that the source item was recolored.

d2: The binding’s “small printed rectangular item” description conflicts with the source image: the item near center appears to be a DVD case/package, while the requested object is the black DVD. This misbinding makes the node assess the wrong object and drives an unjustified unknown. Anchor the comparison to the black disc in the source and evaluate whether that same disc was changed to white in the edited image, using spatial/contextual correspondence and visible appearance; do not require the printed package itself to match either edited disc. Keep unknown only if correspondence genuinely cannot be established. The trace is a valid visual uncertainty, not a transport, schema, or dependency failure; the reference “no” is aggregate guidance, not proof of an atomic label.
